The Little eagle (Hieraaetus morphnoides) is a medium-sized raptor endemic to Australia, occupying a range of woodland and forested habitats across the continent. At hatching, the nestling emerges with a wet weight of approximately 45 grams [Wwb = approximately 45 grams], a relatively modest mass given the species' ultimate adult dimensions. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, by comparison, is recorded at 56 grams [Ww0 = 56 grams], indicating that the embryo deposits a considerable proportion of its egg mass into structural growth during incubation. Eggs incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after a period of 38 days [ab = 38 days], though field records indicate a viable natural range of 37 to 39 days. This incubation duration is broadly consistent with values reported for other Australasian Aquilinae of comparable egg size. The thermal microenvironment of the nest, maintained largely through attentive brooding by the female, is critical to embryonic development; deviations from this optimal temperature regime can extend the incubation period or reduce hatchling viability.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the active breeding season, which frequently involve ambient temperatures approaching 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the developmental timeline of the nestling proceeds through a series of well-defined milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at approximately 59 days after hatching [tx = approximately 59 days after hatching], with reported extremes spanning 54 to 63 days depending on local prey availability and parental provisioning rates at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, follows a considerably longer trajectory; individuals reach gonadal maturation at around 177 days [tp = around 177 days] after hatching, a delay that likely reflects the extended period required to develop the flight musculature, foraging skills, and social competence necessary for independent survival as a breeding adult. at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]The eagle's life history is thus characterized by a relatively slow developmental schedule.

The first successful breeding event for this species typically occurs at an age of approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching], which reflects the time required to secure a permanent territory and establish a pair bond at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The reproductive output of Hieraaetus morphnoides is modest compared to many other raptors of similar body mass. The maximum reproductive rate is realized through a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing 1 to 3 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 1 to 3 eggs]. This corresponds to an annual output of up to 3 eggs per year, translating to a daily rate of approximately 0.0082 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.0082 offspring per day]. This low annual fecundity, characteristic of many long-lived accipitrids, is offset by extended parental care and a high probability of adult survival between breeding attempts. Under laboratory conditions designed to mimic optimal thermal regimes, the processes underlying reproductive activation proceed most efficiently at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the temperature at which the physiological pathways governing gametogenesis and egg formation appear to function at peak efficiency.

Considerable sexual dimorphism is evident in the ultimate adult body masses of this species. Adult females attain a maximum recorded wet weight of 970 grams [Wwi = 970 grams], whereas adult males reach a substantially lower ultimate wet weight of 663 grams [Wwi = 663 grams]. This degree of reversed sexual size dimorphism, in which females are approximately 46 percent heavier than males, is typical among bird-eating raptors and is thought to facilitate niche partitioning by allowing males to pursue smaller, more agile prey while females take larger quarry. The species' lifespan in natural populations is considerable; the oldest documented individual in the wild reached an age of approximately 14126 days [am = approximately 14126 days], though most free-living eagles probably succumb to ecological mortality factors well before attaining such longevity at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. These life-history traits position the Little eagle as a classic K-selected strategist within its guild.

Comparative analysis of growth rates across congeneric species reveals that Hieraaetus morphnoides exhibits a moderately rapid rate of mass gain during the nestling period, driven largely by exogenous provisioning from both parents. The nestling chick transitions from its hatchling mass of approximately 45 grams [Wwb = approximately 45 grams] to its adult female asymptote of 970 grams [Wwi = 970 grams] over a period of roughly two months, an impressive seven-fold increase that requires a sustained delivery of vertebrate prey. Field studies indicate that the fledgling, upon achieving independence at approximately 59 days after hatching [tx = approximately 59 days after hatching], typically disperses from the natal territory within several weeks, although juveniles may remain in the vicinity of the parental home range for up to a year at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Mortality during this post-fledging period is high, with only a fraction of individuals surviving to reach the age of first reproduction at approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching], underscoring the selective pressure on early foraging competence and territorial acquisition at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].
